Description: One of the oldest and most important cities of southern Mesopotamia, at modern Nuffar southeast of Babylon, dominated by the great temple-tower of E-kur, the temple of Enlil, god of the air and chief of the Sumerian pantheon. The University of Pennsylvania expedition begun by J. P. Peters in 1889 uncovered the temple, the ziggurat, residential quarters, and tens of thousands of tablets, making Nippur a cornerstone of Sumerian literature and religion. George Rawlinson proposed Nippur as biblical Calneh, the fourth city of Nimrod's kingdom in Genesis 10:10, citing the Talmudic name Nopher; other scholars prefer Kul-unu, a site near Babylon, or Hursagkalama near Kish, and one recent proposal even reads Calneh as Kalhu (Nimrud). The name Calneh's cuneiform equivalent remains doubtful.
HistoricalPeriod: Sumerian to Parthian, 3rd millennium BC onwards
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: Nippur's own archaeology is secure, but its equation with biblical Calneh is disputed — Rawlinson's Nippur proposal competes with Kul-unu and Hursagkalama, and with a Kalhu reading. ScriptureIlluminated (Genesis 10:10) therefore applies only if the Nippur proposal is right, and the entry is borderline for that reason.
BiblicalSignificance: If Nippur is Calneh, it is one of the four founding cities of Nimrod's kingdom in Genesis 10:10 — the religious heart of Sumer, seat of Enlil, whose archives shaped our knowledge of the world Abraham left. But the identification is only one of several proposals, so the illumination is conditional, and this entry stays borderline.
ArtifactDate: Occupied from c. 5000 BC; ziggurat and temple of Enlil, 3rd-2nd millennium BC
DateDiscovered: American excavations begun by J. P. Peters, 1889-1900
